common_name: Bulgarian Triumph Tomato (Meaty Bulgarian Heirloom Paste Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Bulgarian Triumph is a traditional Bulgarian heirloom bred for meaty, low-seed paste fruit.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Bulgarian Triumph is a traditional heirloom from Bulgaria, bearing medium-sized red fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh well suited to sauce and paste, a style of tomato long favored in Eastern European home gardens for preserving. Its productive, reliable vines yield a heavy crop over the growing season in gardens with a long, warm summer. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture in cooked preparations.

common_name: Cosmonaut Volkoff Tomato (Russian Red Beefsteak Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Cosmonaut Volkoff is a Russian heirloom tomato said to be named for a Soviet cosmonaut, valued for productive, flavorful red fruit.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Cosmonaut Volkoff bears medium-to-large, deep red, round beefsteak-type fruit with rich, well-balanced flavor on vigorous, productive indeterminate vines, a Russian heirloom that has become a steady favorite among tomato collectors for combining classic flavor with reliable yields. It performs well across a range of climates and continues fruiting over a long summer season. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

common_name: Piennolo del Vesuvio Tomato (Vesuvius Hanging Cluster Storage Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Piennolo del Vesuvio is a traditional small red cherry-type tomato grown on the volcanic slopes of Mount Vesuvius near Naples, prized for its thick skin and long storage life.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Piennolo del Vesuvio is a traditional small, oval red tomato grown for centuries on the mineral-rich volcanic soils of the Mount Vesuvius region near Naples, its thick skin and low water content allowing whole trusses to be hung in bunches ('piennoli') and stored through winter without refrigeration, slowly concentrating in flavor as they cure. The tangy, intensely tomato flavor makes it prized in Neapolitan cooking, especially for a quick, bright sauce. Harvest whole clusters when fully colored and hang them in a cool, airy spot to store, checking periodically and using fruit as it continues to ripen.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Corbarino Tomato (Small Campanian Plum-Cherry Preserving Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Corbarino is a small plum-cherry tomato from Corbara in Campania, Italy, traditionally used for sauce and preserving.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Corbarino bears small, oval, bright red fruit in loose clusters, a traditional variety of the Corbara area near Naples valued for concentrated, sweet-tart flavor and thick flesh that holds up well to preserving whole in jars or drying, a regional specialty product in its home area. Its compact fruit size and productive habit make it a good choice for a home preserving garden. Harvest clusters as fruit fully colors for the best flavor.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Pantano Romanesco Tomato (Ribbed Roman Heirloom Slicer)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Pantano Romanesco is a traditional deeply ribbed Roman heirloom tomato named for the Pantano d'Ardea area near Rome.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Pantano Romanesco bears medium-to-large, deeply ribbed red-pink fruit with a flattened shape and rich, complex flavor prized in Roman home cooking for both fresh eating and sauce, the pronounced ribbing and slightly irregular form typical of many traditional Italian heirloom slicers. Its productive vines and well-adapted heat tolerance suit warm growing regions. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Japanese Oxheart Tomato (Meaty Pink-Red Oxheart Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Japanese Oxheart is a large, meaty, heart-shaped heirloom tomato of Japanese origin.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Japanese Oxheart bears large, heart-shaped fruit in pink to pink-red with dense, meaty flesh and few seeds, the classic oxheart form prized for slicing and sauce alike, on productive indeterminate vines. Its rich, well-balanced flavor and substantial fruit size have kept it popular among heirloom tomato collectors. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture.

common_name: Korean Long Hot Pepper (Slender Mild-to-Medium Cooking Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; Korean Long Hot is a slender, pale green pepper widely used fresh in Korean cooking, from mild to moderately spicy depending on growing conditions.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Korean Long Hot produces long, slender, pale to medium green pods with thin walls and mild-to-medium heat that can vary with growing conditions, a staple pepper in Korean cooking eaten fresh, dipped in ssamjang, sautéed, or stuffed. The plants are productive over a long summer harvest season, and pods can be picked green or allowed to ripen to red for a sweeter, hotter flavor. Harvest regularly to encourage continued production.

common_name: Chaotian Pepper (Facing Heaven Chili)

planting.note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; Chaotian, meaning 'facing heaven,' is a small, very hot Chinese chili named for its pods pointing upward as they ripen.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Chaotian bears clusters of small, conical, very hot red chilis that point upward toward the sky as they ripen, giving the pepper its Chinese name, and is a staple in Sichuan and Guizhou cooking, used both fresh and dried in chili oil, hot pots, and spice blends. The compact, heavily fruiting plants produce abundant small pods over a long summer harvest. Harvest continuously to encourage more flowering, or leave pods to dry on the plant for storage.

common_name: African Birdseye Pepper (Tiny Very Hot Piri-Piri Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; African Birdseye is the tiny, extremely hot pepper traditionally used to make piri-piri sauce in southern and East Africa.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since germination is slower and less even than most peppers; transplant only after nights stay warm. African Birdseye produces tiny, upright, intensely hot red pods on a compact, heavily branching bush, the traditional source pepper for piri-piri (peri-peri) sauce across southern and East Africa, later carried by Portuguese traders to become a staple flavoring in Mozambican and Angolan cuisine as well. In frost-free gardens the plant persists as a short-lived shrubby perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual and pick continuously to keep new flowers setting.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Jamaican Hot Chocolate Pepper (Chocolate-Brown Fruity Habanero-Type)

planting.note: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Jamaican Hot Chocolate is a chocolate-brown habanero-type pepper from Jamaica with fruity, smoky heat.

directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Jamaican Hot Chocolate bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen to a deep chocolate-brown, carrying the characteristic fruity, floral habanero aroma along with intense heat and a subtly smoky depth of flavor that distinguishes it from orange and red habanero types. It is a favorite among hot sauce makers for the complex flavor it lends alongside its heat. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; pick pods once fully colored for the best flavor.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Congo Trinidad Pepper (Wrinkled Orange-Red Very Hot Habanero-Type)

planting.note: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Congo Trinidad is a traditional Trinidadian habanero-type pepper with wrinkled orange-red pods and intense heat.

directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Congo Trinidad bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through orange to red, carrying intense heat well into superhot territory along with the characteristic fruity habanero aroma, a traditional variety long grown in home gardens across Trinidad. It is prized for hot sauce and pepper sauce making, where its heat and fruity depth of flavor come through strongly. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; handle ripe pods with gloves.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Bahamian Goat Pepper (Small Elongated Very Hot Bahamian Pepper)

planting.note: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Bahamian Goat is the traditional small, very hot pepper used to make Bahamian goat pepper sauce.

directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Bahamian Goat bears small, elongated, tapering pods that ripen from green to yellow-orange, carrying intense habanero-relative heat and a bright, fruity aroma, and is the traditional pepper behind Bahamian goat pepper sauce, a fiery condiment served throughout the islands with seafood and conch dishes. The compact, productive plants bear heavily over a long warm-season harvest. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest regularly to keep new flowers setting.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Dwarf Wild Fred Tomato (Compact Red Potato-Leaf Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Dwarf Wild Fred is one of the original releases from the international, all-volunteer Dwarf Tomato Project, bred to combine full-size tomato flavor on compact, container-friendly plants.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy, stout stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Wild Fred bears clusters of medium red fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact, potato-leaf plant that stays under 4 feet, one of the early releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project, an international collaboration of home breeders working to create full-flavored heirloom-quality tomatoes on space-saving dwarf plants. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where sprawling indeterminate tomatoes would be impractical. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

common_name: Rosella Purple Tomato (Compact Dusky Purple-Pink Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Rosella Purple is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bred to bring rich, dusky purple-pink 'black' tomato flavor to a compact plant.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Rosella Purple bears medium fruit in a rich, dusky purple-pink, the deep, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomato varieties, on a compact plant from the Dwarf Tomato Project bred to bring heirloom-quality flavor to gardens without room for a full-size indeterminate vine. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

common_name: Summertime Green Tomato (Sweet Green-Fleshed Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Summertime Green is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing sweet, green-fleshed-when-ripe fruit on a compact plant.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Summertime Green bears medium fruit that ripens to a translucent amber-green, the flesh staying green even at full ripeness, with a sweet, mild flavor typical of green-when-ripe tomato types, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant bred to bring specialty tomato flavor to small-space gardens. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where indeterminate vines would be impractical. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint amber blush, since color alone won't signal ripeness.

common_name: Iditarod Red Tomato (Large-Fruited Compact Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Iditarod Red is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bred to produce unusually large red fruit on a compact plant, named for the Alaskan sled dog race.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Iditarod Red bears notably large, deep red beefsteak-style fruit for a dwarf tomato, often rivaling full-size indeterminate slicers in fruit weight despite growing on a compact, manageable plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its combination of big fruit and small plant footprint makes it a standout choice for gardeners short on space who still want a substantial slicing tomato. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

common_name: Perth Pride Tomato (Australian-Bred Red Beefsteak Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Perth Pride is an Australian-bred Dwarf Tomato Project release producing red beefsteak-type fruit on a compact plant.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Perth Pride, developed through the Australian arm of the international Dwarf Tomato Project, bears deep red, beefsteak-style fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact plant, combining full-size tomato quality with a footprint suited to small gardens and containers. It reflects the collaborative, worldwide nature of the Dwarf Tomato Project breeding effort. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

common_name: Sleeping Lady Tomato (Pink-Fruited Alaskan-Named Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Sleeping Lady is a Dwarf Tomato Project release named for an Alaskan mountain, bearing pink fruit on a compact plant.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Sleeping Lady bears medium pink fruit with sweet, well-rounded flavor on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant, named for the Sleeping Lady mountain near Anchorage, Alaska, home to one of the breeding program's participating gardeners. Its manageable size and reliable production suit raised beds and containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

common_name: Katydid Tomato (Green-Striped Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Katydid is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing green-striped fruit on a compact plant.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Katydid bears medium fruit striped green over an amber-green background even when fully ripe, a striking novelty color pattern with tangy, well-balanced flavor typical of green-fleshed tomato types, on a compact plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its manageable size and eye-catching fruit suit raised beds and containers. Harvest when fruit softens slightly, since color alone won't signal ripeness in green-fleshed types.

common_name: Barossa Fest Tomato (Bicolor Red-and-Black Australian Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Barossa Fest is an Australian-bred Dwarf Tomato Project release with bicolor red-and-black fruit, named for the Barossa Valley wine region.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Barossa Fest bears medium fruit blending red and dusky purple-black tones in a distinctive bicolor pattern, combining the rich, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomatoes with the compact habit of a Dwarf Tomato Project plant, developed through the program's Australian breeding collaboration and named for the country's famous Barossa Valley wine region. Its manageable size suits raised beds and containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

common_name: Mr. Snow Tomato (Ivory-White Dwarf Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Mr. Snow is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing pale ivory-white fruit on a compact plant.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Mr. Snow bears medium fruit in a pale, creamy ivory-white with mild, low-acid, sweet flavor typical of white tomato varieties, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant that brings this unusual color to a small-space garden. Its pale fruit stands out strikingly against green foliage and in a mixed harvest basket. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint cream-yellow tone, since it never colors red.
